title: Share your coat (Luke 3:1–20)
hook: John tells soldiers and tax collectors to be fair and share

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy Jesus lost and found in the Temple, and then he grew. Your line was growing is holy. Whose growth did you name out loud? Day four hundred forty-nine, and a new week.

Luke opens chapter three like a historian dating a document. In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Pontius Pilate governor of Judea. Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the next region over, Lysanias of Abilina. Annas and Caiphas the high priests. Emperor, governor, princes, priests: a roll call of power, lined up in order. And then: the word of the Lord came to John, the son of Zachary, in the desert. Not to any of them. To a man in the wilderness.
screen: `THE FIFTEENTH YEAR OF TIBERIUS.` → `A ROLL CALL OF POWER, IN ORDER.` → `THE WORD CAME TO JOHN, IN THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: John comes into the country around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of penance for the forgiveness of sins, just as Isaias had written: a voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare ye the way of the Lord. Crowds come out to be baptized, and he doesn't flatter them. Brood of vipers, he calls them. Don't tell yourselves you're safe because Abraham is your father. The axe is already laid to the root of the trees. And the crowds, shaken, ask the obvious question: then what shall we do? His answer is surprisingly ordinary. In the Douay-Rheims: "He that hath two coats, let him give to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do in like manner." Then the publicans come, the tax collectors, and ask: and us? Don't collect more than you're supposed to. Then soldiers: and what about us? Don't bully anyone, don't accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your pay. Notice what he doesn't say. He doesn't tell the tax collectors to quit, or the soldiers to desert. He tells them to be honest and fair where they already are. The coat in his first answer is a chiton, the tunic worn under the outer cloak. If you have two, one is a spare. Give it away. John's whole preaching points past himself, to one coming who is mightier, whose sandal strap he isn't worthy to untie. And Luke ends the scene with what that honesty cost him: Herod, rebuked by John, shut him up in prison.
screen: `A VOICE CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS.` · `THEN WHAT SHALL WE DO?` · `NOT QUIT: BE FAIR WHERE YOU ARE.` · `A CHITON: THE SPARE TUNIC.` · then, large: `HE THAT HATH TWO COATS, LET HIM GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your spare coat. Settle, and breathe. Picture your closet, or the hooks by your door. Go through it slowly in your mind. Somewhere in there is a coat, a sweater, a pair of shoes, something warm, that you have two of, or haven't worn in a year. Find it. See it clearly. Now think of where it could go: a shelter, a parish clothing drive, a neighbor, someone you know who's cold. Decide. Then, if you like, ask John's crowd's question about the rest of your life: what shall I do, right where I am? If you pray, offer the answer to God. The bell holds the time.
chiton. Greek for the tunic worn under the cloak: John the Baptist told the crowds, whoever has two, give one to someone who has none. Today's word.
Your line: two coats, give one. Today, take the garment you chose and put it in a bag by the door, so it actually leaves the house. Day four hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics hear John the Baptist's preaching in Advent, and some parishes run coat and clothing drives in winter; clothing the naked is one of the corporal works of mercy.

fork.setup: you're a soldier in the crowd at the Jordan. you've heard John's fiery preaching. you ask: and what shall we do? what does he tell you?
options: throw down your sword and leave the army.
do violence to no one, accuse no one falsely, and be content with your pay.
fork.reveal: he doesn't tell them to desert. he tells them to be fair where they are: no bullying, no false charges, no extortion.

original.note: Greek: tunic, the garment worn under the outer cloak; Luke 3:11's 'coat'.

trapdoor: what you thought: John the Baptist was all fire and judgment.
what it means: when the crowds ask what to do, John's answers are ordinary and concrete: share the spare, be honest at work, don't bully.
what a scholar hears: chiton, the inner tunic; and Luke dates John's call the way ancient histories did, by the year of a ruler's reign.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): softened "every powerful name" and "men everyone assumed were crooks"; cut the unsourced "for most people a second one was the spare"; replaced the trapdoor's AD 28-29 dating (not in the text) with how Luke dates the scene; "parishes often" softened.
Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 3:11 quoted from memory; please check.
The answers to publicans (3:13) and soldiers (3:14) are paraphrased; 'a voice of one crying in the wilderness' is given as paraphrase.
Fifteenth year of Tiberius: usually reckoned AD 28/29 (some count from AD 26/27 co-regency). Confirm.
Douay spellings: Isaias, Caiphas, Abilina. Confirm.
Clothing the naked as a corporal work of mercy: standard. Luke 3 read in Advent (2nd and 3rd Sundays, Year C): confirm.
